title: Contest-Winning Microscope Video Revealed as AI Fabrication, Scientists Expose Gizmodo Findings
body:
The winner of Nikon’s 2026 “Small World In Motion” contest has become the centre of a heated debate after the company announced it is re‑examining the entry of Singapore‑based optical engineer Ning Xu. While Xu claimed the striking, ultra‑slow‑motion footage of a single‑cell organism was captured with a conventional Nikon microscope and then “enhanced” using artificial‑intelligence tools, critics argue the final video contains numerous AI‑generated artefacts that misrepresent the underlying biology. Nikon’s decision to launch a formal review underscores growing concerns over the transparency of AI‑assisted scientific imaging and raises questions about how competitions and journals will police the line between legitimate post‑processing and deceptive manipulation.

The 30‑second clip, which earned Xu a $50,000 cash prize and a feature on the contest’s global platform, shows a microscopic worm‑like creature seemingly performing a graceful, almost choreographed series of movements. In a brief statement, Xu explained that he used a neural‑network‑based denoising algorithm to reduce camera noise and improve contrast, a practice that has become commonplace in high‑speed microscopy. However, independent analysts quickly spotted inconsistencies: the organism’s texture appears unnaturally smooth, and several frames seem to repeat or morph in ways that defy known cellular dynamics. A group of bio‑imaging specialists posted side‑by‑side comparisons, highlighting that the AI model likely “hallucinated” structures that were never present in the raw data.

Nikon, which launched the contest to showcase innovative uses of its optical technology, responded by saying it is “carefully re‑reviewing” the submission and will consult external experts to determine whether the post‑processing steps adhered to the competition’s guidelines. The company’s contest rules, updated last year, stipulate that any digital enhancement must be disclosed and must not alter the scientific content of the image or video. “We value integrity in scientific communication,” a Nikon spokesperson said. “If the AI tools used have introduced artefacts that misrepresent the sample, that would be a breach of our terms.”

The controversy arrives at a moment when AI‑driven image restoration is rapidly gaining traction across the life sciences. Machine‑learning models can reconstruct high‑resolution details from low‑light or low‑frame‑rate recordings, enabling researchers to observe processes that would otherwise be invisible. Yet the same power can inadvertently—or deliberately—create misleading visualizations. Recent papers in top journals have sparked debates after reviewers discovered that AI‑generated enhancements obscured critical features, prompting calls for stricter reporting standards. Professional societies such as the International Society for Optical Engineering are now drafting guidelines that require authors to provide raw data alongside AI‑processed outputs and to label any synthetic alterations clearly.

For Xu, the fallout could be career‑defining. The National University of Singapore’s Department of Optical Engineering has placed him on administrative leave pending the outcome of Nikon’s inquiry. In a personal note posted to his professional network, Xu expressed regret over the “misunderstanding” and pledged to make the original, unprocessed footage publicly available. “My intention was to share the beauty of the microscopic world,” he wrote, “not to deceive.” Whether his apology will satisfy the scientific community remains to be seen.

The episode serves as a cautionary tale for both creators and adjudicators of visual scientific content. As AI tools become more accessible, the burden of transparency will increasingly fall on researchers, contest organizers, and publishers to ensure that the line between enhancement and fabrication is clearly drawn. Nikon’s forthcoming decision will likely set a precedent for how future contests handle AI‑augmented submissions, and may influence broader policy discussions on the ethical use of generative technologies in research. In the meantime, the microscopy community watches closely, aware that the next breakthrough image may be as much a product of algorithms as of lenses.
